Header: Plutella xylostella Diamondback moth, 小菜蛾,菜青虫,小青虫, 两头尖 in Chinese

Prevention: Avoid continuous cropping of brassicaceae vegetables in a larger range, because they may all host the pest.
After harvest, immediately clean stubble and leaves because of residual pest eggs.
Plough in autumn, because pupae are in the soil.
Irrigate in winter to reduce overwintering pupae.
Monitoring: The first peak of diamondback moths occurs in mid-May to late
June in northern- central provinces; the second peak occurs in late
For early detection of tiny longish moths use 3 sex pheromone traps/667m2 field.
Look for larvae feeding holes and notches on leaves once a week.
Older larvae feed on the underside of leaves.
At heavy infestation, feeding windows are seen on the leaves.
When many larvae, leaves are eaten up and veins left.
Act quickly when larvae or holes or notches are visible especially at early stage of plant growth.

Thresholds: 1 to 2 larvae every second plant at the seedling stage or rosette stage, 2 to 3 larvae or damaged leaves / every second plant at the early heading period, 5 to 7 larvae or damaged leaves at heading stage.

Solar powered light traps to capture adult moths (3 traps /667m2) at night, on the edge of the field.
Apply botanicals against larvae (such as extracts from staff vine, staff tree or bittersweet
SC 2.5% 多杀菌素悬浮 剂).
Usually applied at 33-50 mL/ 667m 2 , but double- check product labels.
Restrictions: When using a chemical or botanical pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.

Apply no more than 2 consecutive sprays within 5 to 7 days, in the rosette stage of cabbage if threshold is reached.
Avoid application in bright sunlight or into open flowers.
Toxic to aquatic organisms; Low risk to beneficial arthropods.
